tldr: We proposed TERRA, a targeted exploration method that adapts a simulation-pretrained world model to a physical rover at deployment time using prediction errors weighted by task reward sensitivity and a model that predicts those errors. Even on steep slopes under severe out-of-distribution conditions, the physical rover discovered coordinated active-suspension crawling locomotion in just 3 to 5 trials.
hero_caption: The physical ERNEST rover adapting to a steep Mars-simulant slope that differs significantly from its pretraining conditions. It gets stuck during initial trials under conditions where it has never seen a slope (left) or only learned flat-ground driving (right), but TERRA enables it to master active-suspension climbing locomotion within 3 to 5 trials.
overview:
For lunar and planetary rovers to traverse steep slopes and soft ground, advanced control is required to prevent wheel slip and entrapment. Rovers equipped with active suspension can execute crawling motions that crawl forward while shifting ground contact loads. However, phenomena such as soil deformation and rut formation are difficult to faithfully replicate in simulators, so deploying models or policies trained in simulation directly to the real world leads to fatal locomotion failures. Furthermore, long periods of trial-and-error are not acceptable for spacecraft operating under limited power and communication budgets.

To address this, the authors developed TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that explores and learns by zeroing in only on prediction errors that directly affect control performance. Rather than learning all observation dimensions uniformly, it adopts a prediction loss weighted by task reward sensitivity (gradients), and couples the planner with a loss predictor that estimates which action sequences will cause large occurrences of these critical errors. As a result, the system actively selects actions from MPC candidate rollouts that yield data most beneficial for control improvement.

The approach was evaluated under severe out-of-distribution conditions where the rover had zero slope-climbing experience or had only experienced high-friction conditions like flat terrain. In simulation, it reached an approximately 90% slope-climbing success rate within just 5 trials, drastically reducing completion time and energy consumed before the first success compared to baseline exploration methods. In addition, in steep slope experiments on wet Mars simulant using the 75 kg physical ERNEST rover, it autonomously recovered crawling locomotion within just 3 to 5 trials and successfully climbed the harsh real terrain where wheels easily dig in.
contributions: Proposed a parameter-efficient online adaptation method that weights prediction errors based on task reward sensitivity, prioritizing updates on errors directly tied to control performance.

Introduced a loss predictor that estimates future reward-weighted loss along candidate MPC trajectories, realizing self-regulating targeted exploration that guides interactions directly toward task improvement.

Demonstrated high climbing success rates and low energy consumption in simulation under severe settings where pretraining conditions drastically diverged from the deployment environment, and verified that a physical rover recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion in just 3 to 5 trials.

sections.heading: Why Do Rovers Need "Targeted Exploration"?
sections.summary: Future planetary exploration will require venturing onto steep slopes and deformable terrain, but large-scale soil deformation is difficult to replicate completely in simulators. To adapt within limited operational resources, a mechanism that eliminates wasteful trial-and-error and actively resolves only uncertainties tied directly to control performance is essential.
sections.details:
Key targets for scientific exploration, such as steep slopes on Mars or permanently shadowed regions inside lunar craters, are concentrated in extreme, unstructured terrain. On such soft sand and steep inclines, wheel slip and sinkage are severe; in the past, missions have even ended when rovers like Spirit became hopelessly stuck in sand.

To tackle this challenge, JPL developed the four-wheeled experimental rover ERNEST (weighing 75 kg). It features an active gimbal suspension (AGS) with two degrees of freedom connecting the front bogie to the chassis. By coordinating yaw and roll axes, it can alternately shift loads to anchor wheels and pull the chassis upward in a "crawling" gait.

However, when attempting to acquire a policy to properly actuate this multi-DOF suspension via reinforcement learning, solving complex phenomena like soil deformation and wheel rutting in simulation is computationally prohibitive. Consequently, deploying a model pretrained in simulation to the real world inevitably incurs a massive sim-to-real gap.

In space exploration, strict communication delays and power constraints leave no room for dozens of repeated failures. Rather than simply collecting data, the rover must collect only the decisive data that dictates control success or failure within a minimal number of trials. This paper proposes TERRA, a framework that operates a simulation-pretrained world model with Model Predictive Control (MPC) while targeting and adapting only to errors that impact task performance.

captions.F1: Steep slope climbing experiments with the physical ERNEST rover. Because the rover has never seen slopes during pretraining (left) or has only learned flat-ground driving (right), initial attempts fail as wheels sink into the soil. With TERRA adaptation, it successfully masters coordinated active-suspension climbing in just 3 to 5 trials.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Model-Based Adaptation and Intrinsic Rewards
sections.summary: This work is situated within the approach of online adaptation of simulation-pretrained world models at the deployment site. Unlike conventional exploration based on generic model prediction error or novelty, its defining difference is predicting and targeting errors that directly contribute to downstream MPC control performance.
sections.details:
To understand where this research fits, let us organize prior work into several categories:

- Model-Based Adaptation: To improve real-world sample efficiency, methods such as SimDist combine pretrained models with sampling-based MPC and update the model online at deployment. TERRA follows this framework, but differs in that it does not merely minimize overall observation error; it specializes updates on errors that affect the task reward.
- Exploration for Model Learning: Extensive research has investigated providing information gain, prediction error, ensemble disagreement, or novelty (e.g., RND) as intrinsic rewards to explore unknown environments. Self-modeling methods that predict their own errors to encourage exploration also exist. However, conventional methods excessively explore task-irrelevant uncertainties. TERRA's loss predictor predicts reward-weighted loss along candidate action sequences evaluated by MPC, giving it the strength of generating exploration signals directly tied to downstream task improvement.
- Rover Mobility: Traditional terramechanics-based control, methods estimating traversability from visual features, and zero-shot transfer using domain randomization have been studied. In contrast, TERRA plays a complementary role by adapting the world model in an extremely small number of real-world trials when encountering unknown soil mechanics that cannot be fully expressed in simulation.

sections.heading: System Setup and the Overall Framework
sections.summary: This section explains the rover's observation and action spaces, the pretraining process, and the overall TERRA pipeline. Using a Transformer-based world model and a base policy pretrained in simulation, the model adapts online while executing sampling-based MPC in the real environment.
sections.details:
### Platform and Simulation Data
At each timestep $t$, the experimental ERNEST rover receives proprioception (joint angles and velocities), odometry, wheel force sensing, and a local elevation map as observation $o_t$. Action $a_t$ consists of 3 dimensions: commanded forward velocity and AGS target joint angles (yaw and roll). Under a task reward $r^{\mathtt{task}}_t$ that encourages following a goal path while penalizing excessive AGS usage, reinforcement learning is executed in the DARTS simulator, and the resulting transition data is saved as the pretraining dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathtt{sim}}$.

### Model Pretraining and Deployment
During pretraining, a Transformer-based world model is trained to take the past $H$ steps of observation and action history along with a future action sequence to predict observations over the future $T$ steps. Concurrently, a base policy that imitates actions from the simulation policy is prepared to generate initial exploration candidates (warm starts) for MPC.

At real-world deployment, a sampling-based planner called MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) samples numerous candidate action sequences, rolls them out on the world model, and evaluates predicted returns. The observed transition data is immediately added to the deployment dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathtt{deploy}}$, adapting the model online.

captions.F3: The overall TERRA architecture. The pretrained world model rolls out candidate action sequences, while the loss predictor estimates dynamics errors relevant to future control performance. The planner combines the task reward and the targeted exploration reward to determine optimal actions, and immediately updates the model online using data collected from the physical robot.

sections.heading: The Core of TERRA: Reward-Weighted Adaptation and Targeted Exploration via a Loss Predictor
sections.summary: TERRA efficiently updates LoRA parameters using a loss weighted by task reward sensitivity, while simultaneously training a loss predictor that estimates future occurrences of that loss. The planner uses this prediction as an exploration bonus to actively resolve errors tied directly to control.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Performance-Aware Online Dynamics Adaptation
Fine-tuning the entire model on-site causes overfitting and computational latency. Therefore, TERRA inserts Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules only into the Transformer MLP layers and updates only the lightweight parameters $\phi$. In addition, a regularization term $\mathcal{L}^{\mathtt{LoRA}}(\phi) = \sum_i \|\Delta W^i_\phi\|^2_F$ is included to penalize parameter drift, keeping the simulation prior anchored.

Even more critical is the loss function design. Standard prediction error attempts to uniformly reduce errors even in dimensions irrelevant to control, such as distant elevation map errors. TERRA instead weights prediction error using the local sensitivity (gradient) of the task reward with respect to the next state:
$$\mathcal{L}^{\mathtt{dyn}}_{t:t+T}(\phi) = \sum_{k=t}^{t+T-1} \Big( c_1 \|\hat{o}_{k+1} - o_{k+1}\|^2_2 + c_2 \| \nabla_{o_{k+1}} R^{\mathtt{task}}(o_k, a_k, o_{k+1}) \odot (\hat{o}_{k+1} - o_{k+1}) \|^2_2 \Big)$$
The first term maintains consistency across the entire observation space, while the second term prioritizes correcting errors that directly govern the planner's predicted return.

### 4.2 Loss Predictor Estimating Performance-Relevant Loss
To anticipate where critical errors will occur, a loss predictor $g_\psi$ is trained concurrently online. Because continuous regression is easily biased by extreme values, the target loss is discretized into $N$ bins and formulated as a classification problem. Furthermore, to focus on rare states with large errors (such as ground collapse or entrapment), it is trained with a weighted cross-entropy loss ($\mathtt{CE}_w$) that assigns higher weights to high-loss bins.

### 4.3 Exploration-Infused MPC and the Online Adaptation Loop
For each candidate action sequence, the planner (MPPI) selects actions to maximize the combined score of predicted task reward $\hat{r}^{\mathtt{task}}$ and the exploration reward $\hat{r}^{\mathtt{explore}}$ calculated by the loss predictor. Actions likely to yield critical errors receive higher exploration bonuses; as data is collected and errors are resolved, the bonus naturally decays, shifting smoothly toward exploitation. LoRA and the loss predictor are updated immediately at every control step using a batch containing the latest transitions, forming a tightly coupled adaptation loop.

sections.heading: Validation in Simulation and on the Real Rover: Successful Climbing in Just a Few Trials
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted under severe out-of-distribution conditions where the rover had no slope experience or had only learned flat-ground driving. In simulation, it achieved an ~90% success rate within 5 trials, outperforming baselines, and the physical ERNEST rover escaped sinkage and re-acquired climbing locomotion in 3 to 5 trials.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used a steep slope parameterized with M90 Mars simulant soil, which has low wheel-soil shear resistance and easily causes slip. For validation, two extreme out-of-distribution (OOD) pretraining scenarios were prepared:
- No-Slope: Pretraining never exposed the rover to slopes, traversing only obstacles and step terrain (without learning load shifting or slipping on slopes).
- Hard-Ground: Pretrained on slopes, but with soil friction angle set to 60° for an extremely high-grip surface (the rover could climb purely with forward velocity without moving the suspension, never learning coordinated motions).

### 5.2 Simulation Results and Analysis
Across 100 seeds, TERRA reached approximately 90% success within 5 trials under both conditions. Compared to standard exploration baselines like RND, Disagreement, Plan2Explore, and RUNE, TERRA was significantly superior in total actuator energy spent and completion time to first success.

Analyzing error breakdowns revealed that baselines like RND wasted exploration resources reducing errors in dimensions with near-zero reward gradients (such as wheel forces and elevation maps) that barely influence control. In contrast, TERRA selectively minimized prediction error in forward displacement—a dimension directly governing climbing—which explains its high adaptation efficiency. Ablation experiments also confirmed that top performance is achieved only when both reward-weighted loss and loss-predictor exploration are present.

### 5.3 Physical Rover (ERNEST) Demonstration
ERNEST was deployed on a steep slope of wet M90 Mars simulant (where moisture increases cohesiveness, making wheel rutting and digging even more pronounced than in simulation). When running the Hard-Ground pretrained model directly, it kept the suspension locked, spun its wheels, and dug deeply into the soil. With TERRA, however, the rover learned rapidly from failure trials. Within just 3 trials under the Hard-Ground condition and 5 trials under the No-Slope condition, it autonomously generated a crawling gait that swung the front bogie yaw axis widely from side to side while advancing, successfully climbing the slope.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
sections.summary: This method assumes that task rewards are computable during deployment and relies on calculating reward-weighting sensitivities. In addition, the loss discretization bins for the loss predictor are fixed values with room for improvement, making adaptive bin designs a topic for future work.
sections.details:
While TERRA demonstrated dramatic adaptation in remarkably few trials, it operates under several assumptions and limitations.

First, it assumes that the task reward function can be evaluated at deployment and that its gradients (sensitivity) with respect to observations can be calculated. In general robot learning tasks, computing rewards may require external privileged information (such as global localization), and situations may arise where rewards cannot be computed from onboard sensors alone. An extension that learns a latent reward model from partial observations and utilizes its sensitivity is noted as a future direction.

Second, the thresholds (bins) used to discretize loss values when training the loss predictor are set manually. Because this setting directly determines the scale of the exploration reward, an adaptive approach that automatically adjusts bin boundaries to follow evolving online loss distributions is desirable.

sections.heading: Appendix: Safety Constraints, Task Generalization, and Ablation Details
sections.summary: The appendix presents extensive supplementary experiments supporting design choices, including safety constraints for tip-over prevention, generalization to an unseen ripple traversal task, and comparisons with LoRA rank and direct regression.
sections.details:
The appendix reports additional experiments confirming the robustness and design validity of the proposed method:

- Integration of Safety Constraints: Exploration would be counterproductive if the rover tips over. Incorporating a penalty when chassis roll exceeds 10° and hard-rejecting trajectories exceeding 15° in MPPI significantly reduced the limit violation rate from 14.2% to 2.4% without degrading climbing performance.
- Generalization to Another Task (Ripple Terrain): Evaluated on traversing wavy (ripple) terrain on deformable ground in addition to slopes. TERRA outperformed baselines in this task as well, which requires a completely different gait pattern: lifting the front wheels and setting them down behind the crest of the next wave.
- Ablation of Design Choices: Training the loss predictor via direct mean squared error (MSE) regression instead of discrete classification degraded performance. This confirms that weighted discrete classification operates robustly against rare high-loss data, whereas regression overreacts. Furthermore, fine-tuning the full dynamics instead of using LoRA substantially deteriorated performance, validating the efficacy of lightweight low-rank adaptation.

takeaways: Prioritizing the reduction of errors that affect downstream task rewards, rather than reducing all errors uniformly, is the key to accelerating online adaptation by orders of magnitude in extreme environments.

Generic exploration that unconditionally pursues high model prediction error easily squanders resources on task-irrelevant noise or non-critical dimensions, resulting in wasted operational energy for robots.

Freezing the large backbone trained in simulation and updating only lightweight parameters like LoRA online enables fast adaptation while preventing overfitting to sparse real-world data and avoiding catastrophic forgetting.
limitations: Assumes an environment and task design where the task reward and its gradients (sensitivity) can be computed directly from observations at the deployment site.
Loss bin thresholds used for training the loss predictor are fixed, requiring manual tuning when environments or tasks change.
Although safety constraints can be incorporated, safety guarantees are not covered when unknown hazardous events (such as falling off extreme cliffs) lie completely outside the model.
